sections.title: Using the API and developer tools
sections.bodyHtml:
The API, SDKs, command line, webhooks, embedded signing and MCP server are available to you within the permissions of the API key you create. You are responsible for what is done with your keys: keep them off public pages, give each integration only the scopes it needs, and revoke a key you think has leaked. Each key can make 600 requests a minute; past that the API answers with a retry time, and nothing is lost if you wait. Requests that create a document or template need an idempotency key so that a retry never sends twice.

Test keys and test mode are for practice. A document made in test mode is emailed only to the person who sent it, carries a TEST watermark and is left out of your usage and billing. Do not use test documents as real agreements.

sections.title: What a Docustay signature is

A Docustay signature is a simple electronic signature with a strong record: the time, the signer's network address and browser and the wording they agreed to are recorded, and the finished PDF is sealed with a digital signature and ends with a certificate of completion. Docustay does not offer qualified signatures and does not check a signer's identity beyond sending the link to the email address you gave. Whether a particular document may be signed electronically is a question for you and your own advisers. sections.title: 4. Payments
sections.bodyHtml: When you add a payment field to a document, you connect Stripe: Docustay sends you to Stripe's own sign-up page, which creates a Stripe account for your business (if you already use Stripe you can instead sign in to your existing Stripe account and connect it to Docustay; you stay in charge of that account, and you can disconnect it at any time). Docustay charges a platform fee of 2% of each payment collected through a payment field on the Free and Pay as you go plans, and no fee on Pro or Lifetime. On top of that, Stripe sets its own pricing for the connected account, and the connected account pays Stripe's fees as usual. The fee is decided by your plan at the moment the payment is made and is recorded with the payment. If you refund a payment in full, the Docustay fee on it is refunded too. Card details are entered on Stripe's hosted page; Docustay never receives or stores them, only the amount, currency, status and Stripe's reference numbers. You can disconnect at any time: Docustay then stops using the account. Docustay never deletes it; it stays in your Stripe login, where you manage it in the normal Stripe Dashboard.

You can cancel from the Billing page (Manage plan). After cancelling you keep read and download access to sent and signed documents on the Free plan, and you can export everything at any time.

sections.title: 1. Docustay’s role
sections.bodyHtml:
Docustay provides software organisations use to prepare, send, sign and keep documents. This policy covers two different roles, and which one applies depends on whose data it is.

  • The documents and signer details an organisation puts into Docustay (organisation data). The organisation is the data controller. Docustay is a data processor, acting only on the organisation's instructions, under the Data Processing Addendum (see our DPA). If you were sent a document to sign, or an organisation using Docustay holds your name or email address, and you have a question about your information, contact that organisation directly: it decides what to ask you for and how long to keep it. Docustay does not decide that; the organisation does. Section 7 says how to reach us.
  • An organisation owner's or team member's own Docustay account. For this — your login, your account settings, your use of the software itself — Docustay is the data controller, and the rest of this policy describes that relationship.

sections.title: 2. What we collect
sections.bodyHtml:
• Account information: name, email, and sign-in details. On the hosted service we use Firebase for sign-in: your password goes from your browser to Firebase, and we never see or store it. A self-hosted install keeps salted password hashes in its own database.
  • Organisation information: your organisation's name, address, timezone and the settings you configure.
  • Usage information: how you use the product, to fix problems and improve it — error logs, performance data, and which features you use.
  • Billing information: processed by Stripe; we store what plan you're on and your billing history, not your full card number.
  • Organisation data, as a processor: whatever your organisation puts into Docustay: documents and templates, the names and email addresses of signers, the record of each signing (time, address, browser and the wording agreed to), form responses, and payments made inside a document. We process this on the organisation's behalf and do not use it for our own purposes.
  • Payment records: If you collect payments through a payment field, Docustay keeps the amount, currency, payment status, Stripe session and payment references and a receipt link, and the fee charged. Card details stay with Stripe.

sections.title: 3. Sub-processors
sections.bodyHtml:
We use the following companies to help provide Docustay. Each is bound by a contract to protect data at least as strictly as we do, and to use it only to provide their service to us.

  • Railway — Application and database hosting. All data you store.
  • Google Cloud and Firebase — Sign-in and supporting infrastructure. Account email and sign-in identifiers.
  • Stripe — Payments and billing. Billing details and payment references; card numbers go to Stripe directly.
  • Resend — Sending email. Recipient email address and the message.
  • Anthropic — The AI model behind Scribe and Find fields with AI. The text or page pictures of a document, only when a person uses an AI feature, and only for that request.
  • Cloudflare — Delivery of the website and the signing pages, and the bot check on the sign-up page. The visitor's address and browser. Page traffic passes through it in transit.
  • PostHog — Product analytics. Events about how the website and the service are used, tied to an account id, never document content.
  • Google Analytics — Website visit statistics, only after you press Accept in the cookie choice. Page visits and a browser identifier, never document content or signer details.
  • A public time-stamp authority (DigiCert by default) — Trusted timestamp on a signed file. A hash of the document only, never its contents.

The file store runs as software of ours on Railway, so it is not a separate company. Services you connect yourself, such as your own Stripe account, are your own choice and are not on this list. Only the AI model provider receives the contents of a document, and only for a request a person starts. We'll update this list if it changes, and changes are covered by section 9.

sections.title: 4. Security
sections.bodyHtml: We use encryption in transit and at rest where supported by our providers, role-based access controls, optional two-step sign-in with an authenticator app (a workspace owner can require it for everyone), tenant isolation enforced at the database level (Postgres row-level security, applied to every table that holds organisation data — not an application-level check that could be bypassed by a bug elsewhere), backups to a separate location, and a dedicated signing certificate for documents signed through the platform. No system is perfectly secure.

sections.title: 5. Retention and deletion
sections.bodyHtml:
We keep personal information only as long as we need it to provide our services and meet legal obligations, and we delete it when you ask us to.

Your own account. Any signed-in member can delete their own account in Settings → My account. You type your email address, and you need to have signed in within the last 15 minutes. The deletion is scheduled with a 14-day cooling-off period, during which you can press "Keep my account". We email you when you ask, 2 days before, and when it is done. Then your name, email address and other details are erased, your sessions end, and your sign-in identity is removed when no other workspace uses it. Documents you signed stay as the signed record, with your name as you signed it, because they are evidence of an agreement with other people. Documents you were asked to sign but had not signed are removed. A sole owner must hand over ownership or delete the workspace first.

A whole workspace. An owner can delete the workspace in Workspace → Data. The owner types the workspace name, signs in again recently, and confirms that a paid plan ends at once, with no refund for the days left. There is a 14-day cooling-off period, every owner is emailed, and any owner can keep the workspace. Then everything in it is removed, including signed copies and certificates. Before you delete, use Download everything: a zip with each sealed PDF and its audit log.

A signer's details. Staff can look up a person and remove their details from documents that are not signed yet in Workspace → Data → Privacy requests. A document the person already signed is kept as the signed record. A signer who wants their details removed asks the organisation that sent the document; for Docustay itself, write to privacy@docustay.app.

What we keep. A platform record that a deletion happened: a SHA-256 hash of the lower-cased email address (or the workspace id), the date and a request id. It holds no names or addresses. Stripe keeps its own billing records for a paid plan.

Backups. The database is backed up once a day to a separate storage location, and those backups are deleted after 30 days, so deleted data can remain in a backup for up to 30 days. When a backup is restored, we carry out the recorded deletions again so that deleted people and workspaces do not come back. We do not currently test restores on a schedule.

For anything these screens do not cover, write to privacy@docustay.app. We'll complete a deletion request within 30 days unless we're required to keep something by law (for example, financial records).

If you are an organisation owner or team member with your own Docustay account, you can ask us to see, correct, delete or export your account information, or to stop processing it for purposes you haven't agreed to, by emailing privacy@docustay.app; you can also delete your own account in the app (section 5). sections.title: Counting visits to the website

It records, for each page view and each click on a few key buttons: the page, the page you came from, your browser and device type, your screen size and the country your request came from. It sets no cookie, does not store your IP address, and does not follow you to other websites. To tell visits apart it makes a one-way code from your address and browser details; the code cannot be turned back into either.

We do not count anyone who pressed Decline in the cookie choice, whose browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control, or who opted out, and we do not count automated browsers. If you press Accept we also load Google Analytics: see the cookies page.

sections.bodyHtml: This Data Processing Addendum applies whenever Docustay processes personal data on your (the organisation's) behalf, as described in our Privacy Policy, and forms part of your agreement with us when you accept it at signup. sections.title: Scope of the processing
sections.bodyHtml:
Subject matter. Docustay prepares, sends, collects signatures on, seals and stores documents for the organisation that holds the workspace.

Duration. For as long as the workspace exists, and afterwards for the periods in the Deletion or return section below.

Nature and purpose. Storing documents and templates; emailing signing requests, reminders and signed copies to the people named on a document; presenting the signing page; recording the steps of each signing; applying the digital seal and certificate of completion; taking payments through the organisation's own Stripe account where a payment field is used; delivering signed webhook events to the organisation's own endpoints; and, only when a person uses an AI feature, sending that request to an AI model.

Categories of people. The organisation's signers and contacts, and its own team members.

sections.title: What Docustay records about its own processing
sections.bodyHtml:
So that you can see what happened to your data, the product keeps its own records and lets you read them:

  • An audit log of every step on a document, with reports that can be exported as CSV.
  • An access log in every workspace of each view, download and export by your team, which owners and admins can list and download as CSV.
  • An API log of each call an API key made, recording the route and the answer and never the contents of the request.
  • An email log of the messages sent for a document, with delivered, bounced and complained statuses; the matching webhook events carry ids only, never an address.
  • A delivery log for each webhook endpoint, showing every attempt and the answer your server gave.

These records are part of your workspace, so they are covered by the same export and deletion steps as the rest of it.

sections.title: 1. Processing on instructions
sections.bodyHtml: We process personal data only to provide Docustay to you and in accordance with your use of its features — we don't use your signers' data for our own purposes, and we don't sell it.

sections.title: 2. Confidentiality
sections.bodyHtml: Everyone with access to organisation data on our side is bound by confidentiality obligations, and access is limited to what's needed to provide and support the service.

sections.title: 3. Security
sections.bodyHtml: We maintain the technical and organisational measures described in our Privacy Policy's Security section — encryption, access controls, database-level tenant isolation, optional two-step sign-in and backups — appropriate to the sensitivity of the data involved.

sections.title: 3A. The measures, one by one
sections.bodyHtml:
Section 3 refers to the Security section of the Privacy Policy. In plain terms, the product does the following:

  • Isolation between workspaces is enforced in the database with row-level security on the tables that hold organisation data, so a query for one workspace cannot return another workspace's rows even if application code has a mistake.
  • Sign-in. On the hosted service, passwords go from your browser to Firebase and are never seen or stored by us. A self-hosted install keeps salted password hashes. Two-step sign-in with an authenticator app or a passkey is offered to everyone, and an owner can require it for the whole team. Sessions can be listed and ended.
  • API keys carry only the scopes ticked when they are made, can have an expiry and an address allowlist, and are shown once.
  • Webhooks are signed with a per-endpoint secret using the Standard Webhooks headers, and the receiver is told to refuse a changed body, a wrong secret or a timestamp older than five minutes.
  • Signed files are sealed with a digital signature over the whole PDF and end with a certificate of completion that carries a hash of the file. A public time-stamp authority receives only that hash, never the contents.
  • Framing. The embedded signing form can be shown only by websites the organisation has listed, and an ordinary emailed signing link cannot be framed.
  • Backups. The database is backed up once a day to a separate storage location, and those backups are deleted after 30 days.

No system is perfectly secure, and Docustay does not hold a security certification. This list describes the controls that exist; it is not a certification.

sections.title: 4. Sub-processors
sections.bodyHtml: We use the sub-processors listed in our Privacy Policy. We'll give you reasonable notice (via email or in-product notice) before adding a new sub-processor that will handle your data, so you can raise an objection.

sections.title: 4A. How the sub-processors are used
sections.bodyHtml:
The Privacy Policy lists each sub-processor and what it receives. In summary: Railway (application and database hosting); Google Cloud and Firebase (sign-in and supporting infrastructure); Stripe (payments and billing); Resend (sending email); Anthropic (the AI model behind Scribe and Find fields with AI); Cloudflare (delivery of the website and the signing pages, and the bot check on the sign-up page); PostHog (product analytics); Google Analytics (website visit statistics, only after you press Accept in the cookie choice); A public time-stamp authority (DigiCert by default) (trusted timestamp on a signed file).

Services the organisation connects itself, such as its own Stripe account, are the organisation's own choice and are not Docustay sub-processors. On a self-hosted install, the organisation's own mail server is its own choice too.

sections.title: 5. Assisting with rights requests and breaches
sections.bodyHtml: We'll help you respond to a data subject request from one of your signers or contacts (access, correction or deletion) using the tools in Docustay, or directly if asked. In the app, staff can look up a person and remove their details from documents that are not signed yet (Workspace → Data → Privacy requests); a document the person already signed is kept as the signed record. If we become aware of a security incident affecting your data, we'll notify you without undue delay so you can meet your own notification obligations.

sections.title: 5A. Handling a request from one of your signers
sections.bodyHtml:
A signer who writes to you about their information is asking the controller, which is you. The tools for answering them are in the app:

  • Find the person. Workspace, Data, Privacy requests lets staff look a person up by name or email address.
  • Remove their details from documents that are not signed yet. A document the person has already signed is kept as the signed record, because the signed copy and its certificate are the evidence of what was agreed.
  • Export. The workspace's data can be downloaded at any time, and the audit and access logs export as CSV.

If a signer writes to Docustay instead, we point them to the organisation that sent the document, and we help the organisation answer when asked.

sections.title: 6. Deletion or return at the end
sections.bodyHtml: You can export your data at any time. The owner can delete the whole workspace in Workspace → Data: a paid plan ends at once and the days left are not refunded, and there is a 14-day cooling-off period during which any owner can keep the workspace. Then everything in it, including signed copies and certificates, is removed. If an account ends in another way, write to us and we delete the data within 30 days, as described in our Privacy Policy's Retention section. Deleted data can remain in a backup for up to 30 days, and recorded deletions are carried out again if a backup is restored.

sections.title: 6A. Retention and deletion, step by step
sections.bodyHtml:
Whole workspace. An owner types the workspace name, signs in again recently and confirms that a paid plan ends at once, with no refund for the days left. There is a 14-day cooling-off period, every owner is emailed, and any owner can keep the workspace. After that, everything in it is removed, including signed copies and certificates.

A team member's account. Deletion has a 14-day cooling-off period in which the person can press Keep my account.

What we keep. A platform record that a deletion happened: a SHA-256 hash of the lower-cased email address (or the workspace id), the date and a request id. It holds no names or addresses.

Backups. Daily backups are deleted after 30 days, so deleted data can remain in a backup for up to 30 days. If a backup is restored, the recorded deletions are carried out again so that deleted people and workspaces do not come back.

Chat with the assistant. The Scribe chat keeps what was said for the number of days the workspace chooses (30 by default, from 0 to 365; 0 means do not keep). The record of what the assistant changed is kept as part of the activity log.

sections.title: In short
sections.bodyHtml: The Docustay website uses a few small files (cookies) to work, and, only if you press Accept, Google Analytics and PostHog to count visits. If you press Decline, or do nothing, no Google code is loaded and nothing is sent to Google; PostHog then counts the visit without storing anything on your device (no cookie, no stored id), with advertising click ids removed. Separately, we count visits with our own cookieless counter, described below. The signed-in app and the signing pages never load analytics at all. The sign-up page does load a bot check from Cloudflare, described below.

sections.title: Cookies the site needs
sections.bodyHtml:
• Your choice about analytics (docustay-consent): remembers Accept or Decline for a year.
  • Theme (docustay-theme): remembers how you like the site to look.
  • Sign-in: when you sign in to the app, a session cookie keeps you signed in. A short-lived cookie is used while a sign-in with an identity provider is in progress.

These are needed for the site to do what you asked, so they are set without asking.

sections.title: Cookies and browser storage are not the same thing
sections.bodyHtml:
A cookie travels to our server every time your browser asks for a page. That is how the app knows who you are after you sign in, and why the sign-in cookie is marked HttpOnly (a script on the page cannot read it), Secure (it is sent only over an encrypted connection) and SameSite Lax (it is not sent along with most requests that start on another website).

Browser storage is different: the value stays on your device and is not sent to us on each request. We use it for conveniences that do not need our server, such as remembering a theme, the draft of a document you have not sent yet, or the language you chose. Clearing your site data in the browser removes both kinds.

sections.title: Signers: what the signing page keeps
sections.bodyHtml:
If you were sent a document to sign, you do not need an account and the signing page does not load analytics of any kind. It keeps the following in your browser so the page works:

  • A token for your signing session, in sessionStorage, so reloading the page does not lose your place. It is gone when you close the tab; if your browser blocks storage, you open the emailed link again.
  • If the page offers to remember your signature and you leave the box ticked, the drawn signature or initials, in localStorage under your name. Untick the box, or clear site data, and nothing is kept.

The signing record that belongs to the document itself (the time, your address, your browser and the wording you agreed to) is not stored in your browser. It is kept by the organisation that sent the document, as described in the Privacy Policy.

sections.title: The signed-in app
sections.bodyHtml:
When you sign in to the Docustay app, one session cookie (ks_session) is set. It lasts twelve hours for a normal sign-in, and signing out ends it at once. A workspace can also sign people out after a period without activity, and a signed-in person can list their sessions and end them (Two-step sign-in and sessions in the app's security settings). The app does not load Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics or our visit counter.

On a self-hosted install that offers sign-in with your own identity provider, a second cookie (docustay_oidc) holds the state of the sign-in while you are at the provider. It lasts ten minutes, is limited to the sign-in path, and is cleared when the sign-in finishes.

sections.title: Bot check on sign-up
sections.bodyHtml: The sign-up page loads a bot check from Cloudflare (Turnstile). Cloudflare receives your address and browser to tell people from programs. It loads before you make any choice about analytics, because its job is to protect the form, and it is not used for advertising or for counting visits.

sections.title: Analytics, only if you accept
sections.bodyHtml:
If you press Accept on the website, we load Google Analytics 4 (the gtag.js script) and PostHog to count page views and how people arrive. Google receives your address (IP), the page, your browser and an approximate region, and sets its own cookies (_ga and similar). PostHog, which we use for product analytics, stores an anonymous visitor id in a cookie and in your browser's storage, and receives the page, the referrer, your browser and an approximate region; it never sees document contents or names, and email addresses are removed from what it receives. We use them to learn which pages help people and which do not. We do not use them for advertising.

If you press Decline, nothing is sent to Google, and PostHog counts the visit in memory only: nothing is stored on your device, and advertising click ids are removed from what it receives. A browser that sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control is not counted at all.

sections.title: What we do not do
sections.bodyHtml:
• We do not use Google Analytics for advertising.
  • We do not send document contents, signer names or email addresses to any analytics service.
  • We do not load Google code before you press Accept, and we load none at all if you press Decline or make no choice.
  • We do not count visits inside the signed-in app or on a signing page.

sections.title: Counting visits without cookies
sections.bodyHtml: Whatever you choose, the public website counts visits with Umami, open-source software on our own server. It sets no cookie and stores no IP address; it records the page, where you came from, your browser and device type, your screen size and your country. Choosing Decline, sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control, or opening any page once with ?notrack=1 in the address stops even this. Automated browsers are not counted. It never runs in the signed-in app or on a signing page. Details are in the privacy policy.

sections.title: Browser signals we honour
sections.bodyHtml:
Our own visit counter checks the signals your browser sends before it loads. If your browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control, if you pressed Decline, or if you opened any page once with ?notrack=1 in the address, the counter does not load. Automated browsers are not counted either. The check runs in your browser, so the signal is honoured before anything is sent to our server.

The Google tools are separate: they load only after you press Accept, and the Cookie settings link in the footer lets you reverse that choice.

sections.title: Changing your mind
sections.bodyHtml: Use the Cookie settings link in the footer to choose again. Declining deletes the analytics cookies Google set on this site where the browser lets us.

sections.title: Clearing it yourself
sections.bodyHtml:
Every major browser lets you see and delete cookies and site data for one website. Clearing the data for docustay.app removes everything in the table above for that browser. The effects are the ones you would expect: you are signed out of the app, the site forgets your analytics choice and asks again, your theme and language go back to the defaults, and any unsent draft kept in your browser is gone. Documents you have sent or signed are not stored in your browser and are not affected.

Blocking all cookies also works, with one cost: you cannot stay signed in to the app, because the session cookie is how the app recognises you.

sections.title: Embedded and self-hosted use
sections.bodyHtml: Organisations can show the signing form inside their own website, and they can run Docustay on their own server. The cookie list above describes the Docustay website and app. A website that embeds the signing form has its own cookies, which are its own responsibility. A self-hosted install sets the app cookies listed above on its own address, and the website analytics described on this page belong to docustay.app, not to the install.

If the change adds a cookie that is not needed for the site to work, the analytics prompt asks again. This page is general information about what the site does and is not legal advice.
